summary: For 8–9 year olds judging whether a lamp lights in a simple series circuit: the core rule is that a bulb lights only when it sits in a complete, unbroken loop from one terminal of a working cell, through the bulb (both its contacts) and back to the other terminal, with any switch closed. Learners commit to a prediction (lights / won't light), then test, then trace the loop to locate any break. The reasoning is qualitative (is the path closed?), never about current magnitude or brightness. Activities move from live predict-test-repair work to scored sorting of circuit pictures to annotated fault-finding references, with explicit attention to the unipolar, 'used-up current', and 'touching is enough' misconceptions.
misconceptions: Current-used-up / attenuation: thinking the bulb 'uses up' the electricity so the return wire is unnecessary — leads to accepting an incomplete loop.
Unipolar model: one connection to the bulb should be enough to light it.
Believing a bulb merely touching the battery will light without a full path through both its contacts.
Thinking a visible, tidy-looking circuit must work — not checking that every join actually conducts (clip on bare metal, bulb seated).
Assuming more cells or more wire guarantees lighting regardless of whether the loop is complete.

activities.title: Will it light? Predict, test, then trace the break
steps: Look at a circuit and commit out loud (or on paper) to 'will light' or 'won't light' BEFORE anything is powered.
Power the circuit (close the switch, or run a screen model) and compare the result to your prediction.
When a prediction is wrong, trace the loop: follow the path with a finger (or watch a moving dot/marker) from one battery terminal all the way round — note exactly where it stops.
In a repair step, fix the fault you found (close the gap, reseat a loose bulb, move a clip off the plastic coating, or re-route a wire to the correct terminal) and re-test.

Work through a sequence of near-identical circuits where each one differs from the last by a single feature (a gap, a clip on insulation, a flat cell, a bulb not seated in its holder, an extra bulb added into the same loop — use bulbs and a cell matched so that both bulbs visibly light).
activities.insight: A bulb lights when it is part of a complete, unbroken loop from one terminal of a WORKING cell, through the bulb (both its contacts), and back to the other terminal (switch closed). Any single break in the path stops the whole loop; separately, a flat (discharged) cell leaves the loop complete but cannot drive enough current to light the bulb, so that bulb also stays dark. Isolating one variable at a time reveals that, with a working cell strong enough for the bulbs used, loop completeness decides every case in this sequence.

activities.title: Sort the circuits: lights vs won't light
steps: Given a set of clear, unambiguous circuit pictures, decide for each whether the bulb lights and place it in a 'lights' or 'won't light' group.
For each 'won't light' picture, name the fault (gap in a wire, clip on insulation, loose bulb, open switch, both wires on the same terminal, or a flat cell).
Justify at least one judgement by describing the full loop you traced (or the point where the trace stopped).
activities.insight: The judgement is binary — lights or does not — and depends on whether an unbroken loop exists with a working cell. Naming the specific fault for each non-working circuit reinforces that a path break can sit anywhere in the loop, while a flat cell fails for a different reason (no working energy source).

activities.title: Fault-finding reference: where is the fault, and why does the bulb stay dark?
steps: On a single annotated circuit, reveal each marked fault in turn (gap in a wire, crocodile clip on plastic, bulb loose in its holder, flat cell).

For each revealed fault, state in your own words why it stops the bulb lighting — a break means no complete path, while a flat cell means the loop is complete but the cell cannot drive enough current to light the bulb.

Build a checklist of what to check, in order, when a real circuit won't light (e.g. is every join on bare metal? is the bulb seated? is the switch closed? is the cell flat? is there a return path to the other terminal?).
activities.insight: Fault-finding vocabulary: a tidy-looking circuit can still fail if any single join does not conduct, or if the cell is flat. Learners build a systematic diagnostic routine rather than guessing.

activities.title: Counterexample probe: both wires on the same terminal
steps: Examine a circuit where both wires from the bulb go to the SAME battery terminal, so it looks fully connected.
Predict whether the bulb lights and give a reason.
Test (or reveal the result): it stays dark. Then re-route one wire to the OTHER terminal and observe it light.
Explain, by tracing, why the same-terminal version has no return path and so no complete loop.
activities.insight: 'Connected to the battery' is not the same as 'forms an unbroken loop back to the other terminal'. A bulb needs a full path through BOTH its contacts; one connection, or both wires on one terminal, will not light it.

checkQuestion: Here are four circuit pictures: one complete loop, one with a gap in a wire, one where both wires from the bulb go to the SAME battery terminal, and one with an open switch. For each, will the bulb light? How can you tell just by looking, without building it?
checkAnswer: The bulb lights only when there's a complete, unbroken loop from one terminal of the cell, through the bulb, back to the other terminal, with the switch closed. Any gap — a break, an open switch, or both wires on the same terminal (no return path) — means no complete loop, so the bulb stays off. You tell by tracing the loop with your finger.
